R06-D-01: Few observations seem less in need of explanation than the darkness of the night sky. The sun sets and the heavens go dark; what else would they do? Yet for several centuries astronomers who took seriously the idea of an infinite, unchanging cosmos found that darkness genuinely puzzling, and their reasoning deserves to be reconstructed, because its premises once seemed almost beyond question. Suppose that stars are scattered more or less uniformly through boundless space. Then any direction in which an observer looks, pursued far enough, must sooner or later meet the bright disc of a star. Remote stars certainly look dimmer than nearby ones, but the number of stars at each successive distance grows in step with the dimming, so that every shell of space contributes as much light as the one inside it. On these assumptions the heavens should glow in all directions with the brilliance of the solar surface. The first replies tried to rescue the infinite universe by blocking the light. Perhaps clouds of dust between the stars absorbed the glow of the most distant ones. The suggestion sounds reasonable until one follows it through, for dust that absorbs light for long enough is warmed by it, and eventually it glows as brightly as the light it swallows. Over an unlimited span of time, absorption delays the problem; it does not remove it. Other proposals arranged the stars in clusters within clusters, so that lines of sight could slip between them, but these seemed contrived, a geometry invented to answer a single awkward question. The resolution now accepted is both simpler and stranger. The universe we can observe has a finite age, and light, however swift, needs time to cross space. Most directions therefore never terminate on a star, because the glow of sufficiently remote stars is still in transit, and to look far enough out is to look back to an epoch before any stars had formed. The expansion of space contributes a second effect, stretching the light of faraway sources to longer and feebler wavelengths. Neither point needs to be accepted merely because it dissolves the paradox; each is supported by independent lines of evidence gathered long after the puzzle was first posed. It would be an exaggeration to say that the darkness of the night proves that the universe had a beginning. Taken alone, it rules out only one combination of assumptions, namely that space is infinite, evenly stocked with stars and unchanging forever, but that is no small thing. A fact available to anyone who steps outside after sunset turns out to be incompatible with what was, for a long time, the most natural picture of the cosmos. The lesson is less about stars than about observation, for the most ordinary features of experience are not always the least informative; sometimes they seem ordinary only because we have stopped asking why they are as they are.
R06-D-02: The usual story of standard time is a story of order arriving to rescue confusion. Before the railways, we are told, every town kept its own time, set by the sun at its highest point, so that a clock in one town might differ by several minutes from a clock in another only a short distance to the west. Travellers were bewildered, timetables were impossible, and the adoption of uniform zones was simply common sense finally asserting itself. The story is not false, but it misdescribes what was replaced. Local solar time was not a muddle for the people who used it. It was tied to something everyone could see: the sun reached its highest point at noon, and noon meant the same thing in the market, the place of worship and the field. For a community whose dealings were mostly with itself, there was little need to coordinate with anyone else, and a time that matched the daylight was the most sensible time to keep. The differences between towns became a problem only when goods and people began to move between them quickly enough for a few minutes to matter. That is what the railways did. A train leaving one town and arriving at another an hour later could not be scheduled sensibly if each station kept its own noon, and on single tracks a mismatch of a few minutes could put two trains on the same stretch of line. Railway companies therefore began keeping a single time along their routes, and governments eventually followed them, dividing territories into broad bands within which every clock agreed. The change was not everywhere welcomed, and some towns resented being told that noon now arrived when a distant company declared that it had. Within each band, clock noon and solar noon could now differ noticeably, and in places at the edges of a zone they still do. Nothing here suggests that standard time was a mistake. Coordinated schedules saved lives on the railways and made later systems, from telegraph networks to air traffic, workable. The point is that standardisation was not the discovery of a correct time hidden beneath local error. It was a choice to make clocks answer to a network rather than to the sky, made because the network had become more important to daily life than the position of the sun. To call the older arrangement confusion is to judge it by the needs of a world that had not yet arrived.
R06-D-03: For more than a century, the kilogram was a thing. Every measurement of mass in the world, from a pharmacist's dose to a shipping manifest, was ultimately traceable to a single cylinder of platinum and iridium kept under glass near Paris, against which official copies were periodically compared. When the definition was changed in 2019, so that the kilogram is now fixed by assigning an exact value to a fundamental constant of nature, the change was widely reported as the end of arbitrariness: the unit no longer depended on a lump of metal that someone had happened to cast. That description gets the gain slightly wrong. The new definition is no less conventional in one obvious respect: the value assigned to the constant was chosen precisely so that the new kilogram would match the old one as closely as instruments could tell. Nobody wanted bags of flour to change weight overnight. Had the cylinder been cast a little heavier, the constant would have been given a different number. What the redefinition removed was not human choice but dependence on a particular object, and with it a peculiar kind of blindness. The blindness worked like this. When the official copies were compared with the cylinder over the decades, they were found to have drifted apart from it by small but measurable amounts. Either the copies had gained mass, or the cylinder had lost it, or both; but because the cylinder was the kilogram by definition, there was no way, even in principle, to say that it had changed. A standard that defines itself cannot be found wanting. Whatever happened to it, it remained, officially, exactly one kilogram, and the masses of everything else silently moved with it. The world's weights were, in effect, being checked against a ruler that nothing could ever check. A unit tied to a constant does not have this problem. Any sufficiently equipped laboratory can realise the kilogram from the definition, without travelling to a vault, and if two realisations disagree, the disagreement is a fact about the apparatus rather than about the unit. It must be admitted that the apparatus in question is elaborate, and only a handful of institutions can build it; in practice, most of the world still calibrates against physical masses, now traced to these laboratories rather than to Paris. Dependence has not disappeared. But it has become dependence on a procedure that can be checked and repeated, rather than on an object whose changes no one could ever detect.
R06-D-04: It is tempting to treat discarded scientific theories as simple errors, interesting only as warnings. The caloric theory, which held that heat is a subtle, weightless fluid flowing from hotter bodies into colder ones, is a favourite example. We now understand heat in terms of the disordered motion of the particles that make up matter, and nothing like a heat fluid exists. Yet to file caloric under mistakes is to miss what made it, for several decades, the most useful account of heat available, and to misunderstand how the theory that replaced it came to be built. The fluid picture explained a great deal, and explained it naturally. It said why heat moves from hot to cold, as water runs downhill, and why a hot body and a cold one placed together settle at a common temperature. It made heat something that could be counted, conserved and tracked through a process, which encouraged careful measurements of how much heat different substances absorbed as they warmed or melted. Some of the most enduring results of early thermal science were first obtained by investigators who believed in caloric, and an influential analysis of steam engines, which showed that the work an engine can extract depends on the temperatures between which it operates, was framed entirely in its terms. That result survived the theory's collapse. The difficulties were real, and they were noticed early. Observations of cannon being bored suggested that friction could produce heat, apparently without limit, for as long as the boring continued. If heat were a conserved fluid squeezed out of the metal, the supply should eventually have run out. Defenders of caloric had replies, some ingenious and some strained, and the theory survived the objection for decades. It is easy to call this stubbornness. It is more accurate to say that a theory which organises a large body of successful work is not abandoned because of one anomaly, particularly when no rival yet explains everything the old theory explained. None of this is to say that false theories are as good as true ones, or that caloric deserved to last forever. It did, in the end, mislead: it could make no sense of heat turning into work and work into heat, which became central once engines were studied closely. The claim is narrower. A theory can be wrong about what something is while being right about many of the ways it behaves, and those behavioural truths can pass, nearly intact, to its successor. Judging past science only by whether its picture of reality was correct makes its history look like a series of failures, when much of it was a series of partial successes handed on.
R06-D-05: Astronomers cannot lay a measuring tape across the sky, and almost every distance beyond the nearest stars is therefore inferred rather than measured. The method is usually described as a ladder. At the bottom are stars close enough for their apparent shift against the background, as the earth travels around the sun, to be observed and converted into a distance by simple geometry. Among those stars are certain pulsating ones whose rhythm of brightening and fading is tied to their true brightness, so that once the rhythm has been timed, a comparison of true with apparent brightness yields a distance. Such stars can be picked out in nearby galaxies, where they in turn calibrate brighter markers still, among them a class of exploding stars that can be seen across a large part of the observable universe. Critics of the ladder, and many popular accounts of it, dwell on its fragility. Every rung rests on the one beneath, so an error at the bottom is carried, and perhaps magnified, all the way to the top. A small mistake in the geometry of nearby stars would misplace the pulsating stars, which would misplace the exploding ones, which would in turn misplace the remote galaxies whose distances tell us how fast the universe is expanding. On this view the ladder is really a chain, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. The image is apt, but only half of it. A chain fails at its weakest link because each link is tested by nothing except the load it bears. The rungs of the distance ladder are tested by one another. Wherever two methods can both be applied to the same objects, their answers ought to agree, and when they do not, the disagreement points to a fault in one of them. Several of the largest revisions of cosmic distances in the past century came about in just this way, when a comparison between overlapping rungs exposed a hidden assumption, such as the neglect of dust that dims starlight or the confusion of two kinds of pulsating star with one. Interdependence, in other words, is not only a route by which errors travel upward; it is also the means by which they are caught. This is no reason for complacency. Cross-checks catch only the errors that differ between methods; a mistake shared by every rung, or built into a calibration on which all of them rely, would pass each comparison untouched. That is why the present disagreement between the expansion rate measured with the ladder and the rate inferred from observations of the early universe is taken so seriously. It may expose a flaw common to the ladder's rungs, or it may reveal something new about the cosmos itself. Either outcome would be informative, and the fact that the question can be posed so sharply is itself a tribute to how far the ladder has been tightened. A structure that could not be checked could never have produced a disagreement worth arguing about.
R06-D-06: Conservation laws are usually taught as the bedrock of physics. Energy is neither created nor destroyed; momentum lost by one body is gained by another; a spinning skater who draws in her arms turns faster because her angular momentum cannot change. Presented in this way, the laws look like the deepest facts we possess, discovered by patient measurement and accepted because nature has never been caught breaking them. A theorem proved in 1918 by the mathematician Emmy Noether suggests that this presentation, though not wrong, puts the foundations in the wrong place. What Noether showed is that, for any system whose laws can be written in a certain standard mathematical form, every continuous symmetry of those laws corresponds to a quantity that is conserved. If the laws are the same today as they were yesterday, energy is conserved. If they are the same here as in the next room, momentum is conserved. If they do not depend on which way a system happens to be facing, angular momentum is conserved. The conservation laws, in other words, are not separate facts standing side by side; they are consequences of a single kind of fact, namely that the rules of nature do not care when, where or in what orientation they are applied. It is tempting to conclude that conservation has thereby been proved, that energy must be conserved as a matter of logic. That would be a mistake. The theorem converts one question into another; it does not settle either. Whether the laws really are the same at all times is something only observation can tell us, and the theorem ensures that the evidence for the symmetry and the evidence for the conservation law are, in effect, the same evidence. What has changed is the direction of explanation. We no longer say that energy is conserved and leave the matter there; we say that energy is conserved because time is uniform, and we are then free to ask whether time is uniform. That question has teeth. On the scale of the whole universe, which is expanding and so does not look the same from one epoch to the next, the symmetry behind energy conservation is not obviously present, and it is far from clear that a universal law of energy conservation can even be stated there. On the older view this would look like a scandal, a crack in the bedrock. On the view the theorem encourages, it is just what one should expect: where the symmetry fails, the conservation law loses its footing, and the surprise would be if it did not. A principle that once seemed beyond question has become something more useful, a claim whose limits can be foreseen.
R06-D-07: Quantum theory is among the most precisely confirmed bodies of physics ever constructed, and it is also, by the admission of many who use it, a theory that does not quite say what it is about. The difficulty is usually called the measurement problem. The theory's central equation describes a system by a mathematical object, the wave function, which evolves smoothly and predictably for as long as nobody looks. Under that evolution a particle can come to be in a combination, or superposition, of possibilities: here and there, spinning one way and the other. Yet whenever an experimenter checks, the apparatus records exactly one result. The textbook rule bridges the gap by decree: at the moment of measurement the wave function 'collapses' to one of the possibilities, with probabilities that the theory supplies. The trouble is that the rule invokes a notion the theory never defines. A measuring device is made of atoms, and atoms obey the smooth equation; treated as part of the physical system, the device should itself enter a superposition of having recorded each result, rather than recording one. Somewhere between the particle and the experimenter's notebook the smooth evolution is supposed to give way to the abrupt one, but the theory does not say where, or why, or what counts as a measurement in the first place. In practice nothing hangs on the answer, because the boundary can be drawn anywhere convenient without altering the predicted statistics. That is precisely what makes the problem so easy to ignore. The proposed solutions divide, roughly, by what they are prepared to give up. Some modify the smooth equation, adding a tiny spontaneous tendency to collapse that is negligible for single particles but overwhelming for anything as large as a pointer. Others leave the equation untouched and deny that collapse ever happens: every possible outcome is realised, each in a branch of reality that cannot interact with the others, and the appearance of a single result is simply what being in one branch is like. Still others add a further ingredient to the wave function, definite positions for particles at all times, guided by the wave, so that the outcome was settled all along. A widely discussed physical process, in which a system's entanglement with its surroundings rapidly suppresses the signs of superposition, is often offered as a solution in its own right; it explains why superpositions of large objects are never seen, but on most accounts it does not explain why one outcome occurs rather than another. Because these rival pictures agree, in nearly every experiment so far performed, with each other and with the textbook rule, a common response is to call the dispute metaphysics, a matter of taste for people who have finished their calculations. The response is understandable but confused. It treats the textbook rule as a neutral baseline from which the interpretations depart, when the rule is itself an interpretation, and an incomplete one, since it relies on a word it cannot define. Nor are the rivals strictly equivalent: the theories that modify the equation predict small departures from standard behaviour in sufficiently large systems, and experiments of increasing delicacy are now searching for them. None of this obliges the working physicist to choose a side before computing a reaction rate; the theory's practical success is real, and it does not wait on the outcome of the debate. But a theory that works without our knowing what it describes has not thereby been shown to need no description. The measurement problem is not a puzzle from philosophy grafted onto physics. It is a gap in the statement of the physics itself, one that the theory's very success has made easy to step around.
R06-D-08: Physicists have long remarked that several of the numbers fixing the behaviour of matter seem oddly well suited to the existence of anything as complicated as a living thing. Were certain forces a little stronger or a little weaker, the argument runs, stars would burn out too quickly or never ignite, atoms heavier than hydrogen would be scarce, and chemistry would offer nothing as intricate as a cell. How tightly these numbers are really constrained is debated, and some claims of extreme precision have not survived scrutiny. Enough of the pattern has held up, however, to pose a question: why should the constants of nature fall within the narrow ranges that permit observers to exist at all? One family of answers appeals to what is usually called anthropic reasoning. Its modest form makes a point that sounds almost too obvious to state: whatever we observe must be compatible with our being there to observe it. We should not be astonished to find ourselves on a planet with liquid water and a tolerable climate, since observers could hardly have arisen anywhere else; to treat our surroundings as a fair sample of the cosmos would be like concluding that a town's residents are unusually fit because everyone one has met there was met at the swimming pool. In this form the principle is not a theory of anything. It is a warning about bias, and as a warning it is both correct and useful. The difficulty begins when the same reasoning is asked to explain the constants themselves. Consider a lottery. A winner who learns that millions of tickets were sold need suspect nothing: someone had to win, and the winner is simply whoever did. But if only one ticket was ever printed and it won, the winner's existence explains nothing about why that ticket was drawn; it guarantees only that, had it not been, there would be no winner left to wonder. A selection effect does explanatory work only when there are many draws among which selection can operate. Applied to the cosmos, anthropic reasoning dissolves the puzzle of fine tuning only if there are many universes, or many regions of one, in which the constants take different values, and we necessarily find ourselves in one of the hospitable few. Defenders of the approach reply that such an ensemble is not invented for the purpose. Some cosmological theories, developed to address quite different problems, appear to imply a vast number of regions with differing properties, and if those theories are right, the anthropic explanation comes, so to speak, free of charge. The reply has force, but it shifts the burden rather than lifting it. The explanation is now exactly as good as the theory that supplies the ensemble, and since the other regions are, on most versions, unobservable in principle, the evidence for that theory must come from somewhere else. Anthropic reasoning cannot certify its own premise. None of this shows that the approach is unscientific, a charge often levelled against it with more heat than precision. Selection effects are a respectable part of reasoning in every empirical science, and ignoring them produces errors as surely as overrating them does. The narrower lesson is that the modest principle and the ambitious one are different claims and should not borrow each other's credibility. The first is nearly beyond dispute and explains almost nothing on its own; the second would explain a great deal, but only on a condition that the principle itself is powerless to establish.
